stories.title: Patients appeal for stem cell transplant lab at CUH
stories.summary: Patients with blood cancer such as leukemia are appealing to the HSE to reestablish a stem cell transplant laboratory at Cork University Hospital (CUH) to alleviate long hospital stays for them in Dublin and Galway, where stem cell labs are currently located. A lab at CUH was closed in the 2000s over compliance issues. It is estimated an investment of around €27 million would be required to restore stem cell treatment in Co Cork. Dan Sheehan is a dairy farmer from Blarney in Co Cork. In July of last year, he was diagnosed with acute leukemia. Mr Sheehan's treatment was a course of stem cell therapy, but that meant a six-week stay in St James's Hospital in Dublin, one of only two centres in the country providing stem cell transplantation. He is now campaigning for the development of a third laboratory to be located at CUH. Mr Sheehan cites the pressure on the existing unit at St James's Hospital and at University Hospital Galway, and the pressure extended stays at those hospitals put on patients from the south of the country and their families as the main reasons for supporting the re-instatement of the stem cell transplant unit at CUH.

stories.summary: British Secretary of State for Northern Ireland Chris Bryant has called for calm amid the ongoing Drumcree parade stand-off. In a message on the social media platform X, Mr Bryant wrote that his door remains open for talks. "Everyone across Northern Ireland wants a peaceful resolution to the situation in Portadown," he said. "My door remains open and I repeat my calls for people to support further compromise. "I would especially urge calm this weekend. I would also encourage people to ignore calls for more people to come to the area at this time of tension. "Such calls are unhelpful and are likely to put further strain on police resources which are already stretched."

stories.title: PBP proposes tax on millionaires, corporation tax hike
stories.summary: People Before Profit is proposing a new tax on multi-millionaires as well as increasing the corporation tax to 20% as part of its alternative budget package. The document - entitled A Radical Budget for an Affordable Ireland - also proposes a €500 electricity credit for every household funded by a levy on data centres. TD Richard Boyd Barrett said taxing wealth and multinational businesses would raise an additional €45bn to go towards tackling the cost-of-living and housing crises. "The idea of taxing wealth and big business in order to address the cost of living and housing misery is an idea whose time has come. "If we make the multimillionaires and the big corporations and the energy companies and the data centers pay some additional taxes, we can protect people from the housing misery, from the cost-of-living misery," Mr Boyd Barrett said. His party colleague, TD Paul Murphy said the Irish people should not accept being "held hostage to the demands of US corporations that are using Ireland as a conduit to a corporate tax haven".

stories.title: 325m barrels released from oil reserves since March - IEA
stories.summary: The International Energy Agency has said that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from 400 million barrels promised in March. The update came a day after G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the US-Iran war. The G7 did not say whether the 100 million barrels included the outstanding 75 million barrels from the March IEA commitment, or came on top of that. The Trump administration has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in the US and elsewhere. Restricted diesel supplies is one of the consequences of the war in the Middle East, where Iran has been throttling ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for US and Israeli attacks. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, part of the fightback against Russia's strikes, have also affected the market.

stories.title: Israeli officials to question flydubai attack co-pilot
stories.summary: Israeli officials are expected to question the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash a commercial passenger flight from Dubai bound for Tel Aviv, according to a source briefed on the investigation. Disaster was averted on flydubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had stabbed the captain in what Israeli officials have said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying 174 passengers and crew. A reserve flydubai pilot crew travelling on the flight landed the plane at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi Arabian authorities. The co-pilot was transferred yesterday to the UAE, where the source said Israeli officials were expected to question him. The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part in the questioning. Asked whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot, an Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.

stories.title: Parrott ascends to higher plane after uneven journey
stories.summary: Normal service resumed on the Real Betis Balompié social media channels last Thursday. For a month, they had been posting incessantly on Troy Parrott, their analytics and commercial people clearly telling them that there's unprecedented interest coming from over there in Ireland. Production was abruptly halted on this stream of output last week when word reached Seville that an extremely angry civil war was raging among the Irish fanbase - online at least - in the lead-up to the first Israel game. Their post informing their followers that Troy had scored against Israel in the 3-0 victory in Debrecen was delivered in the dry tone of a press release, shorn of the usual giddy, internet meme-speak. But they were back to their old form today, posting pictures of Parrott celebrating with the caption 'Cúchulainn' - not a football man of any desrciption - and comparing him to Brazilian Ronaldo. Parrott had just scored one of the most dazzling individual goals anyone can recall at Lansdowne Road.

stories.title: Fitzmaurice tasked with banishing Galway's nearly man tag
stories.summary: Time will tell whether it's a perfect match but Éamonn Fitzmaurice's appointment as Galway senior manager heightens expectation as to what might unfold across the football scene in 2027. After neighbours Mayo emerged from the pack to end their famine last July, much of the commentariat honed in on the likelihood that Sam Maguire could reside in different homes over the next few years. Galway, naturally enough, will be hoping that a visit comes their way. It will soon be 26 years since the famous trophy wintered in Ireland's second largest county. During Pádraic Joyce's reign they became contenders again, reeled off four Connacht titles on the spin and contested two All-Ireland finals. The first of those saw them come up short against Kerry on a day David Clifford and Shane Walsh underlined their individual brilliance. Two years later and it was a case of one that got away. Admittedly not helped by Rob Finnerty going off early on, the Tribesmen, in a contest that at times skirted with turgidity, looked to have the measure of Armagh. But they lacked the ability to put a foot on the Orchard throat. Joyce's post-match reflections said it all: "It's a sickener, there's no doubt about that. I still have nightmares about it. I said to the boys afterwards, we'll regret it probably until we take our last breath in this world. But we had a great chance. We weren't clinical enough on the day, we didn't score enough. Simple as that." Shortcoming exposed. Sadly for Galway, such deficiencies were again to the fore during Joyce's final two years at the helm. An All-Ireland quarter-final against Meath looked to be swinging the Tribes' way going down the stretch, but the Royals had the greater energy when it mattered.
stories.rssSummary: You can't say that Galway are fully primed to land the big prize in 2027, and whether Eámonn Fitzmaurice can edge them over the All-Ireland line will be closely watched.

stories.title: WSL: Man United beat Liverpool for back-to-back wins
stories.summary: Julia Zigiotti Olme's sixth-minute lob proved enough to earn Manchester United boss Eva Olid a second Women's Super League victory of the season after a 1-0 home win over Liverpool. Zigiotti Olme capitalised on a mistake by Liverpool goalkeeper Khiara Keating and, despite some late pressure by Gareth Taylor's side, United held on to make it back-to-back league wins. After a shaky start under new head coach Olid, the Spaniard has now masterminded four consecutive victories in all competitions with United unbeaten in five matches. This was United's 250th match since the team reformed in 2018 and Olid watched her side mark the occasion with the breakthrough after six minutes. It was a moment to forget for England goalkeeper Keating after her pass out from the back was intercepted by Zigiotti Olme, who composed herself and chipped home in superb fashion. Liverpool pushed for a leveller, but United stood strong to move onto seven points in the WSL.

stories.title: Japan rematch gives Ireland chance to prove a point
stories.summary: Through two games of this five-game international window, we've seen a bit of everything – both good and bad – from Ireland. In terms of the positives, we’ve seen fast starts and an eagerness to play a more expansive and open game. We’ve seen new blood settle well into Test rugby, most notably back row Jemina Adams Verling, and a familiar face settle into a new position, such as Anna McGann in the centre. We’ve also seen Beibhinn Parsons looking back to her best, a brace of tries against Japan last week breaking the Irish women’s record. On the other side of the ledger, we’ve seen two games where Ireland have struggled in the second half; one of which they saw out versus Japan, but the other where they fell apart against the USA. We’ve also seen Ireland struggle to adapt to the interpretation of officials, with 27 penalties and two yellow cards conceded, and five tries conceded with players in the sin-bin.

stories.title: MusicTown celebrates Phil Lynott's life and legacy, 40 years on
stories.summary: Phil Lynott, the much loved Dubliner, musician, lead singer of Thin Lizzy and cultural icon, died forty years ago in 1986. To mark 40 years since his passing, MusicTown at the National Concert Hall in Dublin, supported by Dublin City Council, is presenting a programme of events celebrating and reflecting on his life and times under the title Philo-sophy Talks. The events include talks on his early recordings tonight (Friday October 2nd), a concert in his old school in Crumlin tomorrow (Saturday October 3rd), and an exhibition entitled 'Lost Love Of Romeo' at Studio 10 on Wicklow Street across the weekend. For his old friend and collaborator, the artist Jim Fitzpatrick, this week's events have been an enjoyable trip down memory lane. Celebrated for his unique visual style, Fitzpatrick designed iconic album covers for several Thin Lizzy albums, which are on display. He said that he could "only imagine standing here with Philip Lynott looking at this exhibition. He would be in his element." He went on to say that "Philip was one of those wonderful friends... we were more than just friends, we were collaborators."

stories.title: Teaming up for Tall Tales & Murder on RTÉ One
stories.summary: Full of gags, guns, and gold, Tall Tales & Murder sees want-out car thief Paul (rapper-turned-actor Casey Walsh) and worn-out retirement home nurse Bridget (Ella Lily Hyland) embark on the (mis)adventure of their lives. Joining them are the previously comatose Dublin criminal Grinner (Aidan Gillen), Bridget's icy-yet-amorous boss, The Matron (Aisling O'Sullivan), and Bunny (Brian Doherty), a GAA-obsessed detective who valiantly tries to look out for Paul. A second series is in the works, but as viewers binge season one, Stuart Carolan and Chris Addison tell us about the long road to get the story on screens. [It's] really intense, the market. You've got so many things. There's so much coming out all the time. It's almost like the marketing men have taken over. It's non-stop product. You've got IP. You've got vehicles for stars. You're just on this hamster wheel of trying to [get something made]. If you look at the first episode as a pilot, this might be pilot number 10. (Laughs) There's nine that fall by the wayside. The amount of ones you do, you do all the work, you figure out a whole story for a season, you have so many meetings, you do it all - and then it just falls apart at the last minute. And that's regular, that's quite normal... I've lost count of the amount of times. With this, I think the combination of both of us helped, I think, a lot. That was a big factor. It was a lot of fun as well. Mostly!

stories.title: Are smart bikes worth the hefty price tag? I put two to the test
stories.summary: Journalist Glenn Kelly was sent two smart bikes for the purpose of review. Here, he shares whether the tech-savvy equipment is worth the hefty price tag. With the evenings getting longer and the will to get outside for your daily workout slowly waning, now is the time to be looking at equipment that you can use indoors. As luck would have it, I might have just the machines for you. Home fitness is big business; in fact, according to Fortune Business Insights, it is worth $14 billion globally each year. That means manufacturers are stretching the boundaries of technology to replicate the feeling of outdoor activities from the comfort of your home. With that in mind, I was lucky enough to spend the last month testing two of the best premium exercise bikes on the market to see if they warrant your hard-earned money. NordicTrack and Echelon both compete in the premium studio bike tier through their flagship models, but which machine will win out when we test them on features, build quality and ride performance? Grab your water bottle and read on to find out.

stories.title: Two factors preventing ministers from budget utopia
stories.summary: Rarely has so much cash coalesced with such levels of political angst. These are not the days of austerity when the late Brian Lenihan pledged that swingeing cuts would allow the country to turn the proverbial corner. However, two complicating factors are preventing ministers from entering budget utopia. This first is rising energy costs followed closely by soaring grocery bills. That presents the seemingly strange scenario where the country is getting richer, but households are watching their disposable income shrink. Obviously, the Budget, which will be unveiled on Tuesday, must leave workers and families feeling that they were helped.

stories.title: Gardaí treating death of woman in balcony fall as assault
stories.summary: The woman who died in hospital on Wednesday following a fall from a balcony in north Dublin has been named as Kathleen Carey. The incident, which gardaí are treating as a serious assault, took place near Main Street in Belmayne, Dublin 13 on Monday afternoon. Ms Carey was brought to Beaumont Hospital for treatment and died from her injuries on Wednesday. A post-mortem examination has been carried out, the results of which will determine the course of the investigation. A man aged in his 20s was arrested on Tuesday in connection with the incident. He was released without charge yesterday and a file has been sent to the Director of Public Prosecutions.

stories.title: SDLP selects new candidate for Justin McNulty seat
stories.summary: Councillor Peter Byrne will contest Newry and Armagh for the SDLP in next year's Assembly convention, replacing Justin McNulty. Mr Byrne, a councillor for 10 years, was chosen in a selection convention of party members. He runs a business in Crossmaglen, where he lives with his husband. Following his selection, he said he wants to be "a relentless champion for Newry and Armagh". In an apparent reference to the Drumcree dispute, he added: "If the past week teaches us anything, it is that we need to move forward and do politics differently. "For the SDLP, that means making things work today whilst planning for a new Ireland in the future, and I am looking forward to taking this message to the people of Newry and Armagh in the weeks and months ahead."

stories.title: Bellew Electrical agrees deal with lighting firm Element3
stories.summary: Independent electrical wholesalers Bellew Electrical Group has announced a partnership deal with Element3, a specialist provider of technical lighting solutions for large-scale and complex projects in Ireland and international markets. Element3 will join the specialist division within the wider Bellew Group, strengthening the group's technical capabilities and providing an established platform for further growth in the data centre market. Element3 provides complete design, supply, commissioning and support services across lighting control systems, emergency lighting and lighting distribution. It works on major projects across data centres, healthcare, education, transport and large-scale commercial buildings. It has completed hundreds of large-scale projects including more than 40 data centres across nine countries, giving it extensive experience in one of the fastest-growing areas of electrical infrastructure. Today's announcement follows Bellew Electrical's partnership with Waterland in 2024, when the business secured significant investment to accelerate its growth strategy. The wider Bellew Group has a workforce of over 300 people and generates annual revenues of €130m. It plans to grow revenue to €200m over the next 12 months, supported by organic expansion and further strategic acquisitions.

stories.title: Latvians go to polls in shadow of drone incursions
stories.summary: Latvians are voting in a parliamentary election that is likely to keep power in the hands of pro-Ukrainian Prime ⁠Minister Andris Kulbergs, although deep political fragmentation may complicate the formation of a government. Across the Baltics, including in NATO and European Union member Latvia, many voters are on edge after official warnings of potential Russia aggression and a growing number of airspace incursions related to Moscow's war in Ukraine. Russia says accusations that it is planning to attack NATO are baseless and Western officials say it is not capable of launching a direct assault, but security concerns have weighed heavily in the election campaign. Opinion polls put Mr Kulbergs' centrist United List ahead, with about 14% of votes, but followed closely by the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power. A businessman and amateur rally driver, Mr Kulbergs came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling ‌of incidents in which stray military ⁠drones flew undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths.

stories.title: The full-time whistle can't come fast enough for Ireland
stories.summary: When the final whistle goes in Serbia this evening, Heimir Hallgrimsson and his squad will finally be able to breathe a sigh of relief. The most turbulent and difficult week for Irish soccer since the Saipan psychodrama, more than two decades ago, will be over and the Republic of Ireland may finally be able to get back to some sense of normality. There was trepidation and concern when the Nations League draw was made back in February, but the build-up and fallout from this week's double header has already become far more toxic than anyone could have predicted. Last weekend’s pre-match tensions, where players held two votes on whether or not to proceed with the games, as confusion and rumour circled around the camp, looked, at the time, to be the nadir of the issue but things have continued to escalate. An allegation of racist abuse towards Ireland goalscorer Adam Idah was ruled by UEFA to be inadmissible for review by them because Jayson Molumby did not specifically use the word 'racism’ when reporting the incident. That was followed by Israel captain Manor Solomon’s broadside against Ireland. "We have a country ten times better than theirs, stronger, an amazing country with amazing people. Obviously they hate us. We don’t like them."

stories.title: GPA seeks extra €700 a year per inter-county player
stories.summary: The Gaelic Players' Association (GPA) has asked Government for an extra €700 per player a year in support to help with what their CEO Tom Parsons described as "cost of living pressures". Inter-county players and representatives from the GPA met with Minister for Sport Patrick O'Donovan on Wednesday to seek the increase as part of the association's pre-budget engagement with Government. In total the GPA is seeking an additional €2.8m investment, which would bring support up from €1,800 to €2,500 per player. "Government funding is an important recognition of the extraordinary commitment made by inter-county players to our national games," said Parsons. "The findings presented to the Minister today give a clear picture of the reality behind that commitment. "At a time when the cost of living pressures are bearing down on players, Government has an opportunity to deliver something immediate and tangible for the current generation. We are asking for an additional €700 a year per player, bringing the support to €2,500.

stories.title: Every second counts as Ireland turn towards Israel sequel
stories.summary: After an emotional whirlwind against Austria on Thursday night, Heimir Hallgrimsson feels time will be of the essence for his Republic of Ireland squad to be physically and mentally tuned in for the second of the controversial UEFA Nations League fixtures against Israel. The Boys in Green will be making the trek to Backa Topola in Serbia for what is their 'designated' home game on Sunday. Before the first meeting with Israel in Debrecen, Hungary last Sunday, Hallgrimsson and his team dealt with a set of unique circumstances, from a litany of internal meetings and media scrutiny to a range of pre-match gestures. The latter - including the wearing of black armbands and a non-handshake stance with the opposition - will be repeated tomorrow. Speaking after the 2-2 draw with Austria at Aviva Stadium, Hallgrimsson noted that the fraught nature of the upcoming fixture made it all the more vital that his players recover in time. "That is why I'm saying we need to use every second from now until the game to recover, collect energy and be ready not only physically but also mentally for that game," he said.

stories.title: Frawley marks Connacht debut with match-winning try
stories.summary: Debutant Ciarán Frawley's 77th-minute try helped Connacht open their account in the new United Rugby Championship with a 22-19 victory at Benetton. After the Irish outfit lost at home to Stormers last weekend, Stuart Lancaster’s side were heading for another defeat with Benetton able to open up a narrow two-point lead thanks to Bautista Bernasconi’s score early in the second half. However, Frawley followed up a fine first try for the club with a slick finish after an excellent team move to spark jubilant scenes in Italy after a last-gasp win. Only five minutes were on the clock in Treviso when Cian Prendergast put Connacht ahead, but it sparked a frantic opening 40. Benetton immediately replied through Bernasconi before Sean O’Brien restored the visitors lead, but Leonardo Marin’s try and a successful conversion by Jacob Umaga put the hosts on front with 35 played. Frawley had other ideas with a 37th-minute score backed up with two points by Sam Gilbert and while Bernasconi’s try after 51 minutes ensured Benetton held the lead for long periods of the second half, a brilliant move finished with three minutes left earned Lancaster’s men a bonus-point triumph.

stories.title: On love, loss and belonging in nature - Eoin Warner's new memoir
stories.summary:
In January 1979, when Eoin Warner was two years old, an oil tanker exploded in Bantry Bay. Among the fifty lives lost was Eoin's father. This devastating event cast a long shadow, shaping a childhood in which grief was a quiet presence at the table and in the empty front seat of the car. During this time, Eoin discovered how the natural world reflects so much of our human story, and it became his refuge. This memoir is not a straight line through loss; it's a series of vivid encounters with
the natural world, brimming with enchantment and wonder. In May 2010, a vixen appeared in Booterstown. What was fascinating about this visitor was that she would wander around in the revealing light of day, no doubt driven by a hungry litter of cubs. She would slip along the edge of the path in front of the houses and walk, Houdini-like, through the railings of our gate to visit our garden. We used to watch from the window, enthralled by this wild visitor as she sniffed the empty dog bowl and the hens, who were safe in their run. On one surreal occasion, the vixen even flirted with Mac. Although she was smaller than him, he was delighted by the female attention. They played for ages, running rings around each other on the small lawn. Mac had a bit of a roving eye. A relaxed human leg or a vixen were all fair game in his mind. Adaptation to environmental change is a natural part of evolution, a process that unfolds over generations in which the strongest survive. Unfortunately, in this epoch of human-induced environmental change, the pace is so rapid that many species cannot adapt quickly enough to survive. Some species, however, are adjusting and leveraging the skills they already possess to adapt to this rapidly changing landscape. The red fox (Vulpes vulpes) is one. Their natural range spans extreme climates across the whole northern hemisphere, where they have made almost every habitat their home. Historically, the shy fox has preferred to avoid human contact and has made its home in rural settings. However, as we encroach on the foxes' habitat with our growing towns and cities, making their habitat ours, they adapt, moving into our urban areas. Take a night-time drive at any time of year through the lamp-lit streets of Dublin and you are almost guaranteed to see a fox moving in the shadows. On a warm June evening, the front door was open and the vixen walked into the house, meeting me in the living room. We both stopped dead in our tracks, six feet apart, and stared at each other. I was startled, as I’m sure she was, but if so, she certainly did not show it. She stared at me with emotionless amber eyes, her gaze examining me. Her sharply cocked ears were faced squarely in my direction and didn’t move. She looked incongruous among the brightly coloured blue and yellow toys. Once she grew bored of our staring contest, she turned and left without even a courtesy glance back. It was the strangest feeling, as if this were an affront. The fox has taught me to honour these shared spaces, so that I now acknowledge I am entering another's space – the more-than-human world. Now, whenever I enter a woodland, a bog or the sea, I pause and remind myself that I am the visitor.

stories.title: Carter joins Late Late Show Country Music Hall of Fame
stories.summary: Country music star Nathan Carter has become the latest inductee to The Late Late Show Country Music Hall of Fame. He received the award on The Late Late Show Country Music Special on Friday night, presented by Patrick Kielty. Last year's inductee Sandy Kelly announced Carter as the winner, with his parents Ian and Noreen and his granny Anne later joining him on The Late Late Show couch. Receiving the accolade, Carter said that having his family there was "unbelievable. I just didn't expect it. Thank you so much. It's been 15, 16 amazing years since I left Liverpool and never dreamt (of this)... Starting off in pubs... back here tonight." "Funny enough, we opened with Time of Your Life tonight and that was the first song I sang on The Late Late as a single, 13 years ago." Carter joins previous inductees in The Late Late Show Country Music Hall of Fame including Daniel O'Donnell, Sandy Kelly, Margo, Philomena Begley, Declan Nerney, Susan McCann and Big Tom.

stories.title: Kilkenny bakery makes history at Blas na hÉireann food awards
stories.summary: Arán Bakery & Bistro has been named Supreme Champion at the Blas na hÉireann Irish Food Awards for the second time, making history as the first producer to ever take home the coveted title more than once. The announcement was made at an awards ceremony this evening, as part of a four-day celebration, taking place from 1 to 4 October in Daingean Uí Chúis, Co. Kerry. Now in their 19th year, the Blas na hÉireann awards are famed for celebrating produce from across the country. This year, over 3,000 products from every county in Ireland competed across more than 200 categories. The most notable awards, though, are undoubtedly Supreme Champion, sponsored by Bord Bia, and Best Artisan Producer, sponsored by LEO Network. Arán Bakery & Bistro were crowned Supreme Champion thanks to their "exceptional breads and pastries", which have "consistently impressed" the Blas na hÉireann judges. Having previously been a finalist, gold medal winner and Supreme Champion in 2022, Arán has returned to the top spot four years later with its Arán spelt sourdough – making Bart Pawlukojc and his team the first ever recipients to win the Supreme Champion title twice.

stories.title: Drumcree parade highlights divide in Northern Ireland
stories.summary: The email dropped into my inbox at 2.19pm a week last Friday - 25 September. "The Parades Commission has today issued a determination in relation to a public procession notified to take place in Portadown on Sunday 27 September." So convinced were journalists that the Drumcree parade would be banned - just as it had been 1,476 times over the last 28 years - that many were in Newry for a court case. It was a pre-sentence hearing on former DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson, who has been convicted of a rape and sex offences against two young girls. You could see the ripple of disbelief move through the knots of reporters as they read the determination on the street outside. It had been reduced in size, the time had been changed, other restrictions had been applied, but it was on.

stories.title: Former garda spared jail over coercive control of wife
stories.summary: A former garda who pleaded guilty to coercively controlling his wife has been spared jail after a Judge handed down an 18-month suspended sentence. David Reynolds, from Mullingar in Co Westmeath, was ordered to pay €10,000 to his former wife and complete an anger management course. Judge Keenan Johnson said it was difficult to sentence, because of conflicting factors, but he was moved by the position of the children involved and the negative impact incarceration may have. The judge noted that incarcerating him would separate him from his children, with whom he had a loving relationship. During the sentencing at Mullingar Circuit Court this afternoon Judge Johnson said it was clear David Reynolds had a "gross misconception" of what marriage is. He said it was a significant case of coercive control, which occurred from 1 January 2019 until 18 July 2022.

stories.title: SF alternative budget targets living costs, second homes
stories.summary: Sinn Féin is proposing a permanent ten cent reduction in petrol and diesel as well as extending excise cuts for another six months as part of its €13.4 billion alternative budget package. The 40-page document, entitled 'Putting workers and families first', proposes the Government not proceed with planned carbon tax increases, remove all excise on home heating oil and reduce green diesel by 17 cent for a minimum of six months. The proposed measures to help reduce fuel costs for households run to €1.5 billion with the expense of cutting 10c off petrol and diesel at the pumps for the next year running to €404 million. As per last year, Sinn Féin is proposing an emergency cost of living package. This would include an "Everyday Essential Card" - a preloaded card with €500 for one million households most in need to spend on groceries - and the extension of the back-to-school clothing and footwear allowance to every child in the country. The party would also provide €400 in energy credits for householders. Sinn Féin would also abolish student fees, halt public transport fare increases and introduce a new tier of child benefit to target those most at risk of poverty.

stories.title: Irish Mist sale sees brand return to Irish ownership
stories.summary: Co Offaly-based drinks brand Irish Mist has been sold by US company Heaven Hill Brands to Dublin-based drinks business, the Old Canal Quay Spirits company. The Old Canal Quay Spirits company is owned and led by international spirits industry specialist and entrepreneur David Phelan and fellow Irish drinks industry figures. He is one of the two men behind the sale of the Boru Vodka/Castle Brands which he co-founded with Pat Rigney, from The Shed Distillery, in 1998. stories.title: Widdecombe murder accused charged over Farage terror plot
stories.summary: The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has also been charged with a terror plot against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. Joshua Kerry, 28, is charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts relating to alleged activity between 31 May 2024 and 8 July 2026, Counter Terrorism Policing said. Reform UK spokeswoman and former Tory minister Ms Widdecombe, 78, died on 8 July after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times, a court previously heard. Mr Kerry was arrested on suspicion of murder two days after Ms Widdecombe was found dead. Senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, said: "We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. "The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counter Terrorism Policing network.

stories.title: O'Shea lights up Thomond Park as Munster beat the Bulls
stories.summary: Charlie O'Shea announced himself to Thomond Park with a sensational performance, as the young out-half steered Munster to an impressive bonus-point win against the Bulls in Limerick. The 20-year-old scored two tries and kicked three conversions in his first start for the province, and was given a standing ovation as he departed on 68 minutes following a dazzling performance in Munster’s 26-22 win. His first try was all heart as he charged down a clearance kick from Curwin Bosch before winning a race to the line, before an acrobatic dive to the corner in the second half nudged Munster into a 19-17 lead from which they never looked back. Even before his two tries, the Corkman was catching the eye, sending a stunning crossfield kick to Diarmuid Kilgallen for Munster’s opening try, and drawing a majestic conversion in off the right touchline. Clayton McMillan’s side had to come from 7-0 down early on and trailed 17-14 early in the second half, but they were full value for their bonus-point win as they dominated the final 30 minutes, with O’Shea’s second try and a bonus-point score from Alex Kendellen giving them a much-needed win to kick-start their season, although the head coach will be sweating on more injuries, as Michael Milne (below) limped out in the opening half. The opening minutes were played out largely in the Bulls 22, as two penalties gave Munster the chance to set up camp in opposition territory, although they couldn't make it count as Sean O'Brien's knock-on ended the attack, while an early injury to Michael Milne compounded the frustration.
